newsitem.title: USA: NYC seen releasing Nov budget adjustment shortly.
newsitem.headline: NYC seen releasing Nov budget adjustment shortly.

text.p: New York City, whose tax revenues are running about $289 million higher than it had expected, plans to release its first quarter adjustment to the 1997 fiscal budget as soon as Thursday, city sources said Tuesday.

The sources, who declined to be named, said they did not anticipate any big surprises, though the Giuliani Administration recently has put much more emphasis on issues that are hot in election years, like textbooks for schools.

"In (this) Administration, the November modification is pretty mild and technical," said one of the sources. "In November, there are no surprises," he said, but cautioned that the press and fiscal watchdogs might shock the Administration by finding something it had not anticipated they would criticize.
City sources speculated that the rise in revenues might help the city avoid cutting as much as $500 million, an amount Giuliani has asked city agenies to save.

"I think they're not preparing us for anything, so don't hold your breath," one said, but added this did not mean New York City might not need to take harsher actions in January, which is the middle of its fiscal year.
And he noted the city still is focused on trying to get a new infrastructure authority enacted by Albany, as a way of getting around a constitutional debt limit.

Spokeswomen for the Giuliani Administration declined to comment on the November modification or on the reports of Gov. George Pataki's new welfare program, which he is expected to unveil on Wednesday at 1100 EST.

A spokesman for Pataki also did not disclose whether the governor, whose 1997 fiscal budget was not approved until 104 days after it was due, would release the new plan in December, as he did last year.
"We're still working on that," said Mike McKeon.

New York City has around 66 percent of the state's welfare caseload, and thus is directly affected by the governor's new plans, which include gradually reducing cash benefits over five years, after which they end, newspapers said.

There was speculation that Pataki's plan was so strict, thus likely to prompt such a strong fight from the Democrat-led Assembly, which previously has blocked reforms, that the bill would not be taken up in a special session.

One of the sources, who requested anonymity, said he understood that Pataki would call a special session for the first two to three days of December to give the legislators a pay rise and extend the city's income tax surcharge.

"It will not deal with welfare," he said. The source noted that if the legislature were not called back into session to extend the city's tax surcharge, this could be done retroactively, though this would be unprecedented.
Spokesmen for the governor, and members of the Assembly and the Senate who are involved with welfare refor, either declined to comment or were not immediately available.
Pataki last week said he would only recall the legislature for a special session if there were an agreement or the leaders were close to reaching one.
A city source noted that the Giuliani Administration, which previously has asked Albany to cut welfare and Medicaid programs, saying they were too costly.

"Purely from a fiscal standpoint, the city saves money from the Pataki proposal," he said, though he added that the debate over how generous these public assistance programs should be likely will center on the state's traditional role in caring for the needy. This principle is set forth in Article 17 of the constitution.
